fields.summary: A fast black and white film in production since 1989, made by Harman technology and sold under the Ilford name. Rated ISO 400 and usable well beyond it.

description.text: Tonality is soft and forgiving rather than punchy. The emulsion uses cubic grain, the rounder conventional crystals, where Ilford's own Delta line uses the flatter tabular kind: Delta is the sharper and finer-grained film, and this is the one whose grain reads as texture rather than noise. That is most of why people reach for it. It looks like black and white film rather than a desaturated color photograph.

Harman rates it at ISO 400 and says it will produce high quality prints at meter settings up to EI 3200, the exposure index you set on the camera, given extended development in Ilfotec DD-X, Ilfotec HC, Microphen or Ilfotec RT Rapid. Best results come at 400; good ones are had anywhere in between. Push toward the top and shadows empty out, which some people shoot for deliberately.

Reciprocity is a non-issue across the range most people work in: between half a second and 1/10000, no exposure adjustment is needed at all. Past half a second it needs more light than the meter says.

Ilford calls it ideal for action, available light and general-purpose work, which matches how it gets used: reportage, street, anything where the light changes faster than you can meter. It is the wrong choice when you want fine grain or smooth gradation, where a slower film will do better.

omitted.grain in the datasheet: The Nov 2018 technical information sheet contains no statement about cubic or tabular grain across all six pages. That claim rests on a lab blog, a weaker tier, and is marked as such rather than upgraded.

fixed.citation granularity: The description previously carried one URL under four paragraphs, so a datasheet claim about EI range sat under a lab blog citation. Each paragraph now names the page it came from.
fixed.built to be pushed: Design intent nobody stated. The datasheet says it can produce high quality prints up to EI 3200 with extended development, so that is what the entry says.
fixed.developer names: Cut earlier for want of a source. The datasheet names all four.
fixed.reciprocity: New, and primary sourced. It is the kind of fact a spec sheet cannot carry and a photographer actually uses.
fixed.summary attribution: 1989 belongs to the film, not to Harman, which did not exist until 2005.

fields.summary: A 1998 compact with a 38 to 120mm zoom, sold in some markets as the IQZoom 120Mi. It replaced the Espio 120 and was replaced by the 120SW.
fields.description:
The lens covers 38 to 120mm at f/4.8 to f/12.5, in seven elements across six groups, and focuses to 0.65m. The shutter runs from 2 seconds to 1/400.

Focus is a five point autofocus system. There is no aperture or shutter control: the camera decides exposure and you decide where to stand.

The appeal is size. Pentax fitted a 3.2x zoom into a body close to an Olympus Mju, which is unusual for a zoom of that range. The cost is the long end, where f/12.5 puts you on flash or fast film well before 120mm. It is best treated as a wide-to-normal camera that reaches further when it has to, rather than a zoom you would choose for the long end.

omitted.weight: 208g or 240g depending on the listing, and camera-wiki does not state it. A fifteen per cent spread has no honest coarse form.
omitted.metering, bulb, spot AF, mid-roll rewind: An earlier draft cited camera-wiki for all of these. Reading the page directly, it states none of them. The Pentax manual would restore them and has not been located.

fixed.hedged numbers: The previous draft wrote 'around f/12' and 'no faster than 1/500' to avoid asserting contested digits. That was over-cautious: camera-wiki states f/4.8-12.5 and 2s to 1/400 directly and that page was fetched and read, so the figures are cited and are stated plainly. Hedging a number that is sourced makes it less useful for no gain.

fields.summary: A 1981 SLR on the Canon FD mount, and the model that brought program mode to the AE-1 line.
fields.description:
Program mode is the reason it exists. The AE-1 it followed would pick an aperture once you had chosen a shutter speed; this one picks both, leaning toward keeping the shutter fast rather than the aperture open. Shutter priority and full manual are still there, so the automation is a floor and not a ceiling.

The shutter is an electromagnet-controlled cloth curtain running from 2 seconds to 1/1000. Metering runs from EV1 to EV18 at ASA 100 with an f/1.4 lens on the front, so the low end is a dim room and only with fast glass, and the reading appears as LEDs in the viewfinder rather than a swinging needle.

It came with a split-image and microprism screen bright enough to focus lenses as slow as f/5.6, which matters more than it sounds: a dim screen is what makes a slow zoom unusable on a manual focus body. At 575g for the body alone it has a weight that modern cameras do not, and the lens is a separate decision from the camera in a way it is not on a compact.

omitted.FD lens availability: The draft said FD lenses are plentiful and cheap because they fit nothing made since. Two settleable claims in one sentence, neither sourced.

fixed.first-Canon claim: The previous summary said this was the first Canon to set both shutter speed and aperture itself. That is false: the Canon A-1 shipped in 1978 with programmed AE and Wikipedia calls it the first SLR to offer an electronically controlled programmed autoexposure mode. The claim came from me, not from a source. Wikipedia says program AE was the major difference from the AE-1, and I turned a difference into a superlative.
fixed.metering floor: EV1 is quoted with an f/1.4 lens. Without the qualifier the number promises more than the camera does with the f/1.8 most people have on it.
